To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
both PS2 and PS1 reduce the Ca2+, and that PS2 does this by increasing Ca2+, leakage and reducing Ca 2+ uptake.

1) both wild‐type and familial Alzheimer’s disease mutant forms of presenilin-2 reduce the Ca(2+) concentration of intracellular Ca(2+) stores, 2) the mechanism of action of PS2 is to increase passive Ca(2+) leakage and reduce Ca(2+) uptake by the stores, 3) the mechanism of the increased Ca(2+) leak is the increase in the activity of both IP3- and ryanodine-receptors,

(i) PS2, both wild‐type and mutants, increases passive Ca2+ leak out of the ER; (ii) wild‐type PS2, both endogenous or exogenously expressed, reduces the Ca2+ loading capability of the ER; and (iii) PS2‐D36A mutant, uncleaved and devoid of presenilase activity, mimics these effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of presenilins (PS) on intracellular Ca2+.
the molecular mechanism underlying the role of PS2 as a regulator of intracellular Ca2+.
the role of presenilins in the regulation of Ca2+ homeostasis, which may have implications for Alzheimer’s disease pathophysiology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PS2 protein, both wild type and mutant, reduces Ca2+ storage by increasing Ca2+-leakage and reducing Ca2+-uptake.
the effect of PS2 on store Ca2+ is not mediated by its catalytic activity.
PS2, by reducing the Ca2+ loading capacity of intracellular stores, may be involved in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer’s disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PS2 is able to dampen intracellular Ca2+, both by increasing the Ca2+ leakage from stores and reducing the Ca2+ entry into them.
PS2 is a negative regulator of intracellular Ca2+.
PS2, by increasing the passive leak and by reducing the Ca2+ influx, would lower the Ca2+, and thus, the energy demand of ER.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PS2 is able to regulate the Ca2+ content of intracellular stores by acting on both the Ca2+ influx and the Ca2+ efflux pathways.
, in addition to the well‐known role of PS in the γ‐secretase complex, it can also act as an endogenous inhibitor of the SERCA‐2b pump.

, by increasing the passive Ca2+-leak and reducing the Ca2+ influx through SERCA‐2, PS2 dampens intraluminal Ca2+, thus contributing to the maintenance of low Ca2+ levels in the endoplasmic reticulum.
